segments.text: Hello overflow! Ladies and gentlemen, that's incredible that a lot of young people have come to see how they can shape the future of this continent. Now we are moving to the heart of this morning's conversations, the generational exchange. So ladies and gentlemen, moderating this conversation, put your hands together for my co-host Tania Imani.

Thank you Garikai. Your excellencies, it is now my honor to invite you to stage for the generational exchange. Ladies and gentlemen, please welcome His Excellency Hugues-Alexandre Barrault-Chambriere, Vice-President de la République du Gabon.

The Right Honorable Samuel Nsokwane Matekane, Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Lesotho. And His Excellency Paul Kagame, President of the Republic of Rwanda. I am so delighted and honored to be sat here with our excellencies for such an important moment and conversation.

Since the first Continental Summit here in Kigali in 2017, YouthConnekt has accumulated quite some numbers. It has grown to 39 member states, engaged more than 16 million young people, supported more than 50,000 youth businesses, and helped create over 250,000 jobs. But reach, while commendable, is not the goal in and of itself.

The AIDS Summit asks a much harder question. What do leaders and young Africans owe one another, and what must we build together? So as we start this conversation, I'll just give a few guidelines on how this will all work. I'll put one question, a different question, to each of our excellencies, and I'll have one question for all three of them.

From that point, the floor moves over to you, our young leaders. They'll be roving microphones. When a mic is handed to you, you will say your name, your country, and go straight to your burning question.
So without further ado, let us begin. Your Excellency, Paul Kagame, I would like to start with you. The theme is shaping a generational mission.

What should be the mission of today's generation, and how can young people identify and take ownership of that mission? And what are the consequences if they fail to fulfill that mission? Well, let me start by thanking the Prime Minister, the Vice President for joining us, and let me say hello to you all, the young people. Now, back to the question. I think the young people have to be the ones, first and foremost, to define what their mission is.

I don't think they should be waiting for anybody to give them a handout, spelling out to them what their mission is. But their mission will come from their study and understanding of the history that has brought them up to this point. Therefore, as they look back, they should be able to analyze and say, well, this was for this time, and it has come to affect us this way.

So our role is to make sure that we take it from here and correct what we think needs to be corrected, and play our part, and shape the future as the best way we can. And so, another generation will come and take over from there and continue that. So this must be very clear.

And I think the young people must also understand that there should be no shortcuts. I think they need to invest themselves, work hard, and collaborate across, within countries, or across countries, so that as they cut out this mission, they give it that weight and meaning it deserves. Now, if they fail, you understand the consequences, of course.

I think they will live a life of complaints, of all kinds of struggles that never end, and it comes back to them, because they are the ones who carry the weight of these problems. So I think they must understand that they need to put everything they have in them to make sure that things are put right the way they should, because in the end, they are the ones who benefit. So let me end this particular part of the answer to your question by saying, and I want the audience maybe to think about it, and let's talk about it at the end.

We need some stories here from this audience to tell us, for the last YouthConnekt summits we have had, what they learned and what produced results for them. That's when we shall make sure that we just don't meet, say nice things, and in the end, we go back and do very little, if not nothing. So please, I would be interested in hearing from you testimonies, stories of saying this is how this journey has transformed me, or have shaped me, or have helped me understand, and across the board, how the YouthConnekt has really had its impact, the way it was thought about.
Thank you. Thank you, Your Excellency. Thank you.

And that really speaks to what's at the core of this conversation and this mission, this generational exchange, where young people can study and learn from what has happened, and be able to make better informed decisions going forward, and we definitely take note of your desire to hear more testimonies and stories from our young leaders. Now, moving to you, Prime Minister. You have spent decades building businesses before entering public service.

Africa has the AFCFTA and other commitments on visa-free travel, yet young entrepreneurs still struggle with borders and the cost of transport. What, in your opinion, must our institutions change so young people can actually use these agreements? Thank you very much, Moderator. Let me pay my respects to Nadia Kagame and our Vice President.
Let me start by saying that it is true. I come from business. I was 40 years in business before I joined the public service.
What I want to tell our new entrepreneurs today... Is it not on? It is on. If you can just move it a little bit closer, Prime Minister. Thank you.
What I want to tell our new entrepreneurs today is business is doable, and it's very easy if you allow it to work for you. These are all young people. They are starting this journey today.

Some of them have started some time back, but they are still on the journey of success, because that is where we all want to end up. We all want to be successful business people of now and forever. The journey is not easy.
It's definitely not easy. There's a lot of ups and downs. There's a lot of turbulences which they will face, but they must stay strong because their destination is success.

So they need to stay very strong and focus. Whatever they make in business, they must always put it back into business to make sure that they grow their businesses. In that way, the day when the businesses have grown, they will start their savings.

Put the money aside, because we all know that one day it will rain. So when it rains, you must be able to buy an umbrella. So I'm just trying to tell them that this journey is doable, and I wish them all the best, all of them, all the best of luck, because every business, it doesn't matter what kind of business, it's a business that can make you.
Short story, I have a friend that started selling simba chips at school. He now has factories supplying even outside of our continent. He's grown so big that he can supply everywhere.

So our young entrepreneurs, I am talking this through experience. Whenever you get the first pay, don't chow it. Put it back into business, and put it back into business, and again put it back into business.
Then you'll see the result of your sweat. Coming down to the question, I think what we need to do as a continent is to work together. Take away the barriers wherever they are.

If a Lesotho business person wants to send stuff to Rwanda or to Gabon or to anywhere in the continent, they must be free to do so with no obstacles. We need to take away the obstacles that are hindering our progress. So thank you very much.

Thank you, Your Excellency, thank you. A recurring message here from our two excellencies that have already spoken, the one of no shortcuts, and a message of grit and endurance for our young generation, and of course that of working together as countries, as nations, and as people. Now in directing my next question, Mr. Vice President, Gabon has opened a new chapter in its history, which has aroused strong expectations among young people.

How can the young African generation surpass the legacy of the past to shape its own destiny, and on what levers should Africa rely? Thank you very much, Madam. Thank you, Your Excellency, Mr. President Kagame, Mr. Prime Minister, dear young people. It is a great honor for me to be here today in the name of President Oligingema, who sends his greetings to his brother, President Kagame.

And I would like to say that I came to Rwanda in 1995. At the time I was an administrator at the International Monetary Fund, and I had the chance to meet President Kagame. I can see all the work that has been accomplished since that time, and I would like to pay tribute to President Kagame for his leadership.

In terms of the expectations of our youth, I believe that, as President Kagame said, they are better positioned to tell us their expectations. And we create in Gabon the conditions for them to benefit from opportunities. There are reforms that are being undertaken, first of all to allow them to have better-adapted realities in our countries.

And I salute the good cooperation that we have with Rwanda, where there are many specialized schools and we have a record number of students here in Rwanda. This is South-South cooperation. It is something important for us.

And the youth must actually be trained in professions that have comparative advantages. And all the new technologies, the questions of artificial intelligence. I believe that we want to diversify our country's economy and transform raw materials.
It is no longer a question for us to be wood producers and to transform these resources abroad and to import them again. It is an aberration. It is the same thing for manganese.

We must open Africa, strengthen partnerships, and have an interregional volume of trade that reaches important sizes to conquer foreign markets. A bit in Europe, in Asia, all over the world. And the challenge that we have is to make sure that our youth seize these opportunities to be able to take control, as the Prime Minister said, of the private sector, to be major players in our economy and, whatever their origin, to promote talent, to promote merit.

And this is what will actually allow us to have added value and that we can weigh. But for this, the state has the responsibility to put the environment, has the responsibility to preserve peace. It is something important.
We cannot do anything without peace. And we trust the young generation. They have no choice but to succeed.
To succeed for them, to succeed for Africa. And we are doing our part. Thank you, Madam.

I will now switch to English and continue with my question for all three leaders. If we were together again here in 2063, what is the one fundamental transformation you would wish to see in the lives of Africans? I will start with you, President Kagame. Well, we need to see change in the relationship we have with, for example, the rest of the world.

We want to see development take hold. We want to see prosperity. And we want to see the Africans not always being at the receiving end of the generosity of the rest of the world, because we've been there too long.

We've been there in a way that it's painful to see that Africans, to succeed, to be given their place they deserve to be, is something that has to be validated by somebody else. I mean, we just have to stop this. We can't go... And it has almost been taken for granted that Africans, and I hope the youth will really change this sort of mentality, where everything African has a validation process that goes through by somebody somewhere else, and it has almost become a permanent state.
We need to break this cycle, without a doubt. So, for those who will be there in 2063, I might be there by the way. At least, we really need to be there, proud and saying, change has happened.

And it has happened on the basis of our efforts, and working together, and making sure that we do ourselves proud, in as far as the Africans have created their place, their space, which... And by ourselves, which we can't keep getting handouts on everything. We are being fed, we are being... Every time it's... You know, we are really so much put in our place all the time, which is very demeaning. I think these young people should be unhappy about it, and do something about it.

They need to work together, they need to know that in them, there is what they need, and equal to what other people have in themselves, that has raised them to a level above us, when it shouldn't be. It shouldn't be. So, let me stop here.
Thank you very much, Your Excellency. Poignant remarks there. I will ask the same question to you, Prime Minister.

If we were together again in 2063, what is the one fundamental transformation you would wish to see in the lives of young Africans? Thank you very much. I think I want to see a different Africa. Africa that has been grown, Africa that has been transformed by our same young entrepreneurs.
Because the truth is, Africa has everything. Africa can sustain itself. What we lack, I think what we lack is a proper way of working together.
This continent, it can easily be transformed by itself, by these young people. I agree with the President, I also believe we'll be there. 2063, we'll be there.

Excellent. So, everything is in our hands, to make sure that, because you'll find that even the people that come out of the continent, they come because we have something that they need, which they don't have. So, let's take advantage of that, our young entrepreneurs.
Let them start taking advantage of that and use it for their benefit. Use it for the continent, the benefit of the continent. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Prime Minister. If we meet here in 2063, what transformation would you like to see in the lives of young Africans? I would like to see a prosperous continent. I would like to see young leaders in all sectors who can assert themselves.

I would like to see a low unemployment rate, the decline of poverty. I would like to see, within our most remote territories, that we can take care of ourselves to train young people, to care for them, and that this coexistence of generations is important. That we can take control.

As President Kagame said, there are aspects of sovereignty and we don't need to ask permission to do, to exploit our resources as best as we can. It's something important, that we are more solidary. And with the dynamics of regional markets, of continental markets, we can start to weigh on the world economy.

With the mastery of technology, we will have an impact to improve productivity, the productivity of work. Use technology to be even more competitive. And from there, we will have a more prosperous Africa, where we can travel from Kigali to Libreville, where we will have opportunities to do so, to settle, to strengthen, and to have an Africa that will be prouder.

2063, what an outstanding vision. We have a redefined relationship with the world. We have increased cooperation, prosperity, an Africa built by Africans, an Africa built by the young people in this very room.

And it's on that note that we open up the floor to you. We'll start off with three young people that are going to set the pace of this conversation. I'd like to call up Tatenda, if you can bring a mic to Tatenda, she's over there, and she will pose the first question.
If you can give your name, your country, and your burning question. Thank you very much, Tanya. Good morning, Your Excellencies.

My name is Tatenda Kerina Jobko, a lawyer and a program specialist from Zimbabwe. AI and emerging technologies are changing how we learn, work, and create, yet much of the technology shaping our future is developed elsewhere, and many African countries are facing gaps in infrastructure, research, and investment. What must African governments, businesses, and young innovators do together to ensure that Africa can become an owner and a creator of these technologies, rather than merely a market for them? Thank you.
Thank you, Tatenda. We'll go to our next pacesetter, Linda, who is on this side of the room. Good morning, Your Excellencies.

My name is Linda Shachinda, founder of PV Beat Farms, a youth-led manufacturing business from rural Zambia under the UNDP ECOWAS project. Your Excellencies, as a Zambian manufacturer already exporting to Botswana and Congo, one of our biggest challenges has been logistics. Getting our products from Zambia to neighboring countries can be expensive and unpredictable.

We may have access to preferential tariffs, but that doesn't necessarily mean we can afford to get our products to those markets, and we have seen what is possible. Through the Nigeria and Rwanda Air Cargo Initiative, eligible exporters have been able to access freight rates for under $2 per kg to selected African destinations. So my question is this.

What would it take to expand such arrangements like this across Africa, bringing in governments, airlines, logistic operators together so that a young manufacturer like me from Zambia or Rwanda or any other country can access affordable and reliable transport to African markets? Thank you. Thank you, Linda. And I believe I have a question from Danny.

Danny, if you can rise, give your name, your country, and your burning question. So thank you very much, Your Excellency, dear young people. My name is Danny Vassili-Modisha, a young Rwandan innovator and spokesman for the French-speaking Parliament of Young People, which brings together young speakers from all over the French-speaking space, including, of course, Gabon and Rwanda.

Your Excellency, as COP 31 is coming to an end, our generation is worried about the lack of cooperation in climate action. Africa is the region that has the least access to early warning systems, while it is one of the most affected. For a farmer or a city threatened by floods, an early warning separates the disaster from security.

Young African innovators are ready to build these solutions. Your Excellency, while African countries are investing in climate action, how can we guarantee open access to data so that young developers can design warning tools in the countries in need? And how can African countries work together in favour of climate action? Thank you very much. Thank you very much, Danny.

So we have our three initial questions. I will direct the first question on AI, which is how do young innovators get a real voice, that we move away from being consumers but actually play a role in being creators? I would like to direct this question to you, Your Excellency Kagame. And then the next question is the air cargo question from Linda.

How do we scale affordable threat solutions for entrepreneurs and businesses across Africa, combining government, private sector and players? And I would like to direct this question to you, Prime Minister. So we will start with you, Your Excellency. Yeah.

On this part of technology and artificial intelligence, I want to inform the audience, and you all know already, by the way, most of these technologies, much as we talk about them being developed in many other places and affecting us in a way, most of those companies that are behind these advanced technologies, actually among their employees, there are Africans. So that is to begin with. So under the talent we have on the continent, I mean, on the continent, we have engineers, we have data analysts, we have, you know, vetters of all kinds.

I think the problem will be addressed by the cooperation which has been talked about by many other people, and even in this discussion, between the private sector, governments, and these talented people who have all kinds of skills and knowledge, and they need to come together. And Africa, we need to have development in infrastructure, as we continue training our people, but we also need to have access to finance. All this is possible.

There is no reason why Africa should be disconnected from this, when we actually have all these things. The only thing we need to do is to come together, deploy them, develop them, and so that they work for us. So we shouldn't be talking about it like, again, as I said earlier, as if these things belong elsewhere, and they only come to us because we have asked or begged to have them come here.

I think there should be collaboration, first among the Africans, secondly, Africans with the others, the rest of the world, of course. And these partnerships should be strong, should be on a level basis. I mean, we can't always be the junior partners in everything.

I think we have to be equal partners at one point. So the task is upon us again, the young people, the governments, the private sector, in between all the kinds of skills needed, you find them. So I think we are waiting for ourselves.
That's all. So I think that is, that facial intelligence, of course, I mean, a lot has been talked about it. It is advanced, it is advancing very fast.

It holds a lot of opportunity. It addresses many problems, but it has a lot of dangers as well. So we have to make sure that we manage this well, maximizing on the benefits, whether it is in medicine or agriculture or transport or different things we need, AI is the way to go.

But we need to put in place certain protections that will minimize the dangers they carry with them. So that, whether it is, we have to emphasize the safety, the privacy, and all things related with that. So I think all this is doable.
People need to sit down and think through it genuinely with single-mindedness to deliver what you want. It's possible. Thank you very much, Your Excellency.
A very clear message and a call for greater collaboration. It is possible. Prime Minister, the next question on air cargo and how we can scale affordable freight solutions for businesses.

I think what we need to take advantage of, we as a continent, we have got a vehicle called African Continental Free Trade Area. If we can use that vehicle, we would be able to make everything possible. But before we get that, before we get to that, we as a continent, our laws, the policies, they should be enabling policies that would make businesses run without any problems.
We need to do that. We have that vehicle which is still there idling and doing nothing. We need to come with the laws and policies that will enable this to work.
The sooner we do that, the better. Thank you. Thank you, Prime Minister.

Poignant remarks there and a clear call to action. I would like to underline President Kagame, to make this data available to farmers, to those who can, with their talents, take advantage of this data, of this information, for an agriculture that will allow to improve yields and anticipate some harmful effects. So, all this work is underway to secure this data, which could be stored in other places where it shouldn't be.
But this work is in progress. There may be cooperation with other countries that are in demand. There are still possibilities for strengthening cooperation.

And our young people have the capacity to embrace these new jobs which offer significant opportunities. Thank you, Mr. Vice-President. What I take away from your answer is that the work is in progress.

And I really appreciate the call to the people in the room that there are opportunities for new jobs. that has a burning question. Raymond, if you could stand up, say your name, your country, Nigeria, and give us your burning question.

Good morning, Your Excellency. Thank you so much for this opportunity. My name is Raymond Okpane from Nigeria, and I am the founder of Youth Spark Pan-Africa, a youth-led organization that is empowering young people, entrepreneurs in the areas of leadership development, innovation, and capacity building.

And most recently, we have focused on providing access to global opportunities for the young people. And I speak as someone who has been coming to Rwanda since 2019. I've been a very consistent participant at the YouthConnekt Summit.

And YouthConnekt has really impacted on the work that we have done or we are doing. And after my very first experience in 2019, I made up my mind that I must get other young people to come and experience the excellence and the results-oriented leadership here in Rwanda. And every year, even when YouthConnekt is happening, I go out of my way to mobilize young people from across continents, members of my community, to come and experience the event.

Now, there are three areas that the YouthConnekt Summit has so much impacted on our community. One of them is in the area of expanded visibility. I remember the first time I came in 2019, we needed to pay a visa fee, $30, to be here.

And I was so surprised that by the time I was coming back in 2020, which was a COVID year that every country was closing down their borders, Your Excellency, you, on that same year, opened up your borders and removed visa fee from all nationalities. And I think that that was very incredible because while other people were preventing other people from coming in, you allowed everybody to come in. And since then, we have kept coming.

So that access to that expanded visibility made that I had to keep inspiring other people to come here to learn from the Rwandan story, and it has greatly impacted on their business. Nobody who has ever come here in our community has ever gone back the same way they came. Now, the second area is in the area of partnership.

I can tell you that we have enjoyed maximum partnership opportunities from the Rwandan government, from the Ministry of Youth, great support from Dr. J.N. Abdala, the Minister of Youth and Arts, Honorable Paula Ngabire, and the former Minister of Youth, Honorable Rosemary Mbabazi. So we have enjoyed great partnership. Rwanda has opened up their arms.

But my fulfillment is that it wasn't about me. Those hands they opened trickled down to supporting the people who believed me enough to put down their money, save money, take permission, put down their resources to come and learn from the Rwandan story. And today, most members of my communities traveled back to their countries and they relocated to live here.

I can tell you, Your Excellency, that some members of the Yusufa community are currently living and doing business right here in Kigali. And even right here as we speak in this auditorium, right over there we also have some members of the Yusufa community as well who have also come from different parts of the world to also be here. And some of them are also going to explore the opportunities to create and also expand their businesses here.

And lastly, Your Excellency, the last area that YouthConnekt has impacted on our community is in the area of relationship building. I remember that in 2019 you were telling us at the BK Arena on the three areas that you had to use to build this country when you started. And I also, you asked a question on what was the priority, what did you have to do first and what did you have to do second? And you said that when you started, there was absolutely nothing on ground and so everything became a priority.

And so that is also the mindset that we have used in our community, such that nothing is being left or said this is better than the other or this is more important. And it has inspired the rate at which we work hard, expanded our vision, which is the first thing that you used to build this country. You said that the first thing you did was to have a vision and you had to influence unity, bring everybody together.

And lastly, you had to think big. Your Excellency, I can tell you in the last two years I came back here and the kind of infrastructure and everything I've seen here is something I've not seen. I mean, I'm so inspired to see them.

But thank you so much for the opportunity. I will keep coming here, I will keep looking for a way to partner and to be a big supporter and partner to what the YouthConnekt is doing. Thank you so much, Your Excellency.

A round of applause, ladies and gentlemen. What a poignant testimony as we were just asking, just demonstrating what this gathering has done in particular. We're talking about increased collaboration, visibility, partnerships, exposure that leads to relocation and mindset reshaping.
Thank you so much, Raymond, for sharing that. I would like to take perhaps two more voices from the audience. If you can say your name, your country, and go directly to the question.
I will take a question here from the front. Do we have the microphones? Yeah. Okay, there we go.
Hello everyone. My name is Isidore Tameu, President of the Chamber of Young Entrepreneurs of Cameroon. This is my first time in Kigali.

I am extremely proud of what I see, because Rwanda today is an example of resilience. It is an example for Africa and for African youth. Today, we are talking about this youth who must transform Africa, rewrite African history, and inspire the world.

Today, I am very proud of the message that Rwanda sends across Africa, and I would like African youth to participate in rewriting history and African culture beyond our borders. Today, I would like the Rwandan model to inspire generations, because we know that to know where we come from, to know where we are going, we must know where we come from, and where we come from is our culture. As a music producer, manager, and very involved in cultural and creative industries, I would like African youth to take ownership of their culture, to open their borders.

Today, Rwanda has opened its borders to Africa, and this is very inspiring. Today, I would like that beyond opening our borders, we must be able to consume local, consume our culture, and be proud of our culture. I would like, for example, that Rwandan artists can create collaborations, not only regional, but also intra-African, that Rwandan culture can be listened to in Cameroon.

I would like that there can be Rwandan stars in cinema, in music, who can inspire artists and collaborate with artists from Central Africa. I would like, for example, that young people who can inspire our culture can be highlighted, highlighted, beyond Africa. And in this dialectic, it is a question, it is a request, an indolence, for President Paul Kagame, who is an inspiration for youth in terms of models, dynamism, transformation, and leadership, to be able to carry the voice of the creators, of the cultural and creative industry, so that Africa can no longer be left behind, so that through the cultural and creative industries, we can have a new look, a new look at South Africa, at its youth, which can inspire the world, which can transform the image we have of the world.

It is a shame that it is by coming to Rwanda that I realize that Rwanda is beautiful, that Rwanda is clean, that Rwandans are disciplined. Yet, through art, through culture, through music, we can have a new look at who we are and be able to impose this new look on the world. I would like that we can carry the role of an Africa that respects its creators, that at the level of the African Union, we can inspire African nations to have statues for artists, so that they can be creators of wealth.
Thank you. Thank you very much. Thank you for this meeting.

Thank you for Rwanda. Thank you very much from our brother in Cameroon. As I prepare to pursue my Master's in Public Policy, I am personally committing to deepening my understanding of policymaking, seeking mentorship and finding evidence-based solutions to existing community challenges.

Now, with that being said, in return, in the name of translating youth participation and into more of involvement and active involvement into the implementation, my request to more of our institutions is this. Can we have clearer pathways to youth-developed policies to receive formal consideration, mentorship from experienced policymakers and for there to be active youth involvement in the implementation process? Thank you. Thank you very much, Audrey.
Okay, with your permission, Excellencies, I'd just like to take one more question and then we'll proceed to the answers. Just the lady here with the microphone. Please go straight to your question.
Good morning. Good morning. I'm Luciana from Mozambique.

First, I want to thank the Excellency President Paulo Cagamey for the good job he did at Cap Delgado using Rwanda Defense Force. Now, we have too many young people investing at Cap Delgado by this cooperation of Rwanda Defense Force. Me, I'm an activist.
I'm also an entrepreneur. I'm holding my card here. Anyone that wants to connect with me can come and take my card.
Okay, thank you. We appreciate the enthusiasm. Would you like to state your question? I have a question, also a suggestion for the Vice Minister.

He told that we, as young people, we can shape Africa doing business. I have a friend at Lesotho, Ethiopia, Zimbabwe. They request things from Mozambique, but the logistic barriers, they can't allow me to do business there.

I would like to ask the President, even the Vice Minister, to consider this, to make the flight ticket low for the entrepreneurs that are registered. Because I understand that the borders must be a safe place, can't allow anyone to come without a certificate or Alvara. In Mozambique, we call Alvara the certificate that makes the person that is paying taxes.
This company pays taxes at some countries. So I think that this can help Africa to develop and to be the Africa that we want. Thank you.
Thank you very much. Thank you. Great remarks and questions.

A lot of praise, a lot of feedback, a lot of testimonies, which is exactly why conversations like this matter. Now, in collecting some of the questions and the insights, I'd like to pose them as follows. I'll start with you, Mr. Vice President.

On the question that comes up several times, how can we set up systems that will allow young entrepreneurs to travel from one country to another? We're talking about costs, fees, taxes. That's the first question. The second question will be directed to Your Excellency, President Paul Kagame.

It wasn't a direct question, but I would like to frame it in a question in how we can increase more artist collaboration, music, the arts. How can we get more collaboration going on the continent? And lastly, I would like to pose the question to clear a pathway for youth involvement in policy and decision-making to you, Prime Minister Mataka. So we'll start with you, Mr. Vice President.

Thank you very much. I wanted to say that it's great to see how our young people are creative. And we have the testimony here that when we put them together, the emulation means that we have testimonies that are very important.

And I really wanted to congratulate Rwanda for the success of this session and say that Gabon is also ready for the next sessions. And I would be happy to welcome this youth. In any case, we are ready.

Now, in relation to the issue of fees and costs, we also have cooperation with Rwanda today and FLA and Gabon, which must facilitate traffic even more. And we are moving forward in the framework of the CEAC for free traffic. I remind you that we are members of the Economic Community of Central African States.
So we have to work. We have demography for us. Demography is our asset.
It's our youth. Because youth is an asset when there is aging in other continents. There is aging.

It's up to us to capitalize on this, to create the environment for our young people, for the free movement of goods and people, to advance all these reforms of the ZLECAF. And from there, we will be able to solve the problems. But we understand that we have to go fast.

We have to avoid promising for the long term things that we can do today.
